title: What fractions mean
summary: Find out what the two numbers in a fraction tell you, and why 1/5 of a pizza is less than 1/3.
objective: Name the fraction of a shape that is shaded and tell which of two pieces is bigger.

hook.prompt: You can have \( \tfrac{1}{3} \) of a pizza or \( \tfrac{1}{5} \) of the same pizza. Which gives you more pizza?

options.feedback: 5 is bigger than 3, but cutting a pizza into 5 pieces makes each piece smaller.
Both are one piece, but the pieces aren't the same size.

hook.explanation: Cut a pizza into 3 pieces and each piece is big. Cut it into 5 and each piece is smaller. Let's see why.

bricks.title: The bottom number: how many pieces
bricks.body:
A **fraction** is part of a whole that's cut into **equal** pieces. The bottom number is the **denominator**. It tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.

Cut a pizza into 3 equal pieces: one piece is \( \tfrac{1}{3} \), one third. Cut it into 4: one piece is \( \tfrac{1}{4} \), one quarter. Cut it into 5: \( \tfrac{1}{5} \), one fifth. More pieces means smaller pieces!

term.definition: The bottom number of a fraction: how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.

visual.alt: Two same-size bars. One is cut into 3 equal pieces with one shaded, labeled one third. The other is cut into 5 equal pieces with one shaded, labeled one fifth; its shaded piece is smaller.

bricks.prompt: This bar is cut into equal pieces. What fraction of it is shaded?

visual.alt: A bar cut into 6 equal pieces, with 1 piece shaded.

options.feedback: That counts only the white pieces. The bottom number counts all the equal pieces: there are 6.
That's upside down. The number of pieces goes on the bottom.

bricks.hint: Count every piece, shaded and white. That number goes on the bottom.
bricks.explanation: The bar has 6 equal pieces, and 1 is shaded, so the shaded part is one sixth.

bricks.prompt: Both rectangles are cut into 4 pieces. Which one is cut into quarters?

visual.alt: A rectangle cut into 4 pieces of different sizes, from thin to wide.

options.feedback: These 4 pieces are different sizes. A fraction needs equal pieces, so these aren't quarters.

visual.alt: A rectangle cut into 4 pieces that are all the same size.

bricks.hint: Look at the size of each piece, not just how many there are.
bricks.explanation: Quarters are 4 **equal** pieces. Only this rectangle has 4 pieces that are all the same size.

bricks.prompt: Two cakes are the same size. Your friend gets \( \tfrac{1}{8} \) of one cake. You get \( \tfrac{1}{4} \) of the other. Who gets the bigger piece?

options.feedback: 8 is bigger than 4, but a cake cut into 8 pieces has smaller pieces.

options.text: Nobody: both pieces are the same
options.feedback: You each get one piece, but cutting into 8 makes smaller pieces than cutting into 4.

bricks.hint: Which cake is cut into more pieces? Are its pieces bigger or smaller?
bricks.explanation: Your cake is cut into 4 pieces and your friend's into 8. Fewer pieces means bigger pieces, so your quarter wins.

bricks.title: The top number: how many you have
bricks.body:
The top number is the **numerator**. It counts the pieces you have.

This chocolate bar has 8 equal squares. You eat 3 of them, so you ate \( \tfrac{3}{8} \), three eighths. The 8 is all the squares; the 3 is the ones you ate.

When the top and bottom are the same, like \( \tfrac{8}{8} \), you have every piece: the whole bar!

term.definition: The top number of a fraction: how many of the equal pieces you have.

visual.html: 38
visual.alt: A chocolate bar of 8 equal squares in 2 rows of 4, with 3 squares shaded, labeled three eighths.

bricks.prompt: A pizza has 8 equal slices. Sam eats 5 of them. Pick the numbers to finish the fraction.
bricks.template: Sam ate [[top]] out of [[bottom]] slices, so he ate [[top2]]/8 of the pizza.

mistakes.feedback: 3 is how many slices are left. Sam ate 5.
Don't add the numbers. The pizza has 8 slices in all.
8 already sits on the bottom. The top counts the slices Sam ate: 5.

bricks.hint: The top is the slices Sam ate. The bottom is all the slices.
bricks.explanation: Sam ate 5 of the 8 equal slices, so he ate five eighths of the pizza.

bricks.prompt: This chocolate bar has equal squares. What fraction of it is shaded?

visual.alt: A chocolate bar of 5 equal squares in a row, with 2 squares shaded.

options.feedback: That puts the white squares on the bottom. The bottom counts all the squares: 5.
That's the white part. The top counts the shaded squares: 2.
That's upside down. All the squares go on the bottom, the shaded ones on top.

bricks.hint: Top: how many are shaded? Bottom: how many squares in all?
bricks.explanation: 2 of the 5 equal squares are shaded, so it's two fifths.

bricks.prompt: A cake is cut into 6 equal pieces. You eat \( \tfrac{6}{6} \) of it. How much cake is left?

options.text: None: you ate the whole cake

options.feedback: The top 6 means you ate 6 pieces. That's all 6 of them, so none are left.
When the top and bottom are the same, you have every piece, not half.

bricks.hint: Look at the top and bottom numbers. Are they the same?
bricks.explanation: You ate 6 of the 6 pieces. That's every piece, so the whole cake is gone.

challenge.prompt: Ava and Ben have pizzas of the same size. Ava eats \( \tfrac{3}{4} \) of hers. Ben eats \( \tfrac{3}{8} \) of his. Who ate more pizza?

options.feedback: 8 is bigger than 4, but Ben's pizza is cut into more pieces, so his slices are smaller.
They both ate 3 slices, but the slices aren't the same size. Ben's are smaller.

challenge.hint: Both ate 3 slices. Whose slices are bigger?
challenge.explanation: Both ate 3 slices. Ava's pizza is cut into 4 and Ben's into 8, so Ava's slices are bigger, and she ate more.

takeaways: The bottom number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.
The top number tells how many of those pieces you have.
More pieces means smaller pieces, so 1/8 of a cake is less than 1/4 of it.
When the top and bottom are the same, you have the whole thing.
